items.prose: A gardener plants a tulip bed of 4 different varieties, chosen from the 8 varieties she has. The 4 go in a row of four spots along a path. She then edges the bed with stones of one colour, chosen from 4 colours.

parts.question: How many ways can she choose the 4 varieties, ignoring which spot each one takes?

feedback.generic: Not quite. The spots do not matter yet, so each group of 4 should be counted once.

byKey.ordered: That is $8 \times 7 \times 6 \times 5$, which counts every order of each group. Divide by the $4! = 24$ orders.
byKey.divide-four: You divided by 4. A group of 4 can be ordered in $4! = 24$ ways, so divide 1680 by 24.
byKey.times: You multiplied 8 by 4. Choosing 4 of 8 is $\binom{8}{4}$, not $8 \times 4$.

explain.text: In order there are $8 \times 7 \times 6 \times 5 = 1680$ picks. Each group of 4 appears in $4! = 24$ of them. So there are $1680 \div 24 = 70$ groups.

parts.question: Once the 4 varieties are chosen, in how many orders can they be planted in the four spots?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Fill the spots one at a time and multiply the choices left.

byKey.four: That counts the varieties, not their orders. The first spot has 4 choices, the next 3, and so on.
byKey.repeats: $4^4 = 256$ lets a variety fill two spots. Each variety is planted once, so it is $4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1$.

explain.text: The first spot takes any of the 4 varieties and the second one of the 3 left. Then 2 are left, then 1. That is $4! = 24$ orders.

parts.question: Using 70 groups and 24 orders for each group, how many different rows can she plant?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Each group can be planted in each of its orders.

byKey.added: You added 70 and 24. Every group goes with every order, so multiply: $70 \times 24$.
byKey.carried: That is $1680 \times 24$, from 1680 groups in part 1. With 70 groups the rows number $70 \times 24 = 1680$.

explain.text: Choose the group, then the order: $70 \times 24 = 1680$ rows. This matches filling the spots straight from 8 varieties: $8 \times 7 \times 6 \times 5 = 1680$.

parts.question: Using 1680 rows, how many different beds are there once the colour of the edging stones is chosen too?

feedback.generic: Not quite. The edging colour is one more stage after the row.

byKey.added: You added the 4 colours. Every row can take every colour, so multiply: $1680 \times 4$.
byKey.no-order: That is $70 \times 4$, which ignores the order of the spots. Use the 1680 rows: $1680 \times 4 = 6720$.
byKey.carried: That is $40320 \times 4$, carried from a slip earlier. With 1680 rows it is $1680 \times 4 = 6720$.

explain.text: The edging is a stage with 4 choices, whatever row was planted. So the beds number $1680 \times 4 = 6720$.

items.prose: A coach lines up the 7 players of a netball team in one row to be introduced before a match. The captain must stand in the middle place. The two shooters are twins and must stand side by side.

parts.question: Ignore both rules for now. In how many orders can the 7 players stand?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Fill the places in turn and multiply the choices left.

byKey.square: $7 \times 7$ lets a player stand in two places. The choices go down by one each place.
byKey.seven: That is the number of players. The orders multiply the choices for every place.

explain.text: There are 7 choices for the first place, 6 for the next, down to 1. So $7! = 5040$ orders.

parts.question: Using the 5040 orders, how many of them put the captain in the middle place?

feedback.correct: The other six players fill six places: $6! = 5040 \div 7 = 720$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Put the captain in the middle first, then fill the other places.

byKey.not-middle: That is $5040 - 720$, the orders with the captain somewhere else. We want her in the middle.
byKey.six: That counts the six other players, not their orders. They fill six places in $6! = 720$ ways.

explain.text: With the captain fixed in the middle, the other 6 players fill 6 places in $6! = 720$ ways. Each of the 7 places holds the captain equally often, so this is also $5040 \div 7$.

parts.question: The captain stands in the middle. Which way of counting the twins' rule is right?

options.text: Count the side-by-side pairs of free places: two on each side of the captain, so 4 pairs.
Glue the twins into one block and arrange it with the other four players: $5! \times 2$.
options.why: That treats the six free places as one row. The captain splits them into two rows of three, so a block cannot sit across the middle.

options.text: Count the side-by-side pairs of places in the whole row: 6 pairs.
options.why: Two of those 6 pairs use the middle place, which the captain already holds.

options.text: The twins cannot stand together once the captain is in the middle.
options.why: There is room for them. Places 1 and 2, for example, are side by side and both free.

feedback.correct: The captain splits the free places into 1 to 3 and 5 to 7. The pairs are 1-2, 2-3, 5-6 and 6-7.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Think about which pairs of places are both free and side by side.

explain.text: The captain takes place 4 and splits the free places into 1 to 3 and 5 to 7. Each group of three has 2 side-by-side pairs, so there are 4 pairs. A glued block would also allow places 3 and 5, which are not side by side.

parts.question: Part 2 found 720 orders with the captain in the middle. Using the 4 side-by-side pairs of free places, how many of those 720 also have the twins side by side?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Choose the pair of places, then the order of the twins, then fill the rest.

byKey.block: That is $5! \times 2$, the glued block, which lets the twins stand either side of the captain. Count the 4 pairs instead.
byKey.no-swap: You placed the twins one way only. Either twin can stand on the left, so multiply by 2.
byKey.pairs-six: That uses 6 pairs of places, including two that need the middle. With 4 pairs it is $4 \times 2 \times 24 = 192$.

explain.text: Pick one of the 4 pairs of places for the twins, then put them in it in 2 orders. The other 4 players fill the 4 places left in $4! = 24$ ways. So $4 \times 2 \times 24 = 192$ orders.

items.prose: A five-a-side football league has 8 teams. In a season every team plays every other team twice: once at home and once away.

parts.question: How many different pairs of teams are there?

feedback.generic: Not quite. A pair is two teams with no order, so each pair should be counted once.

byKey.ordered: $8 \times 7 = 56$ counts each pair twice, once in each order. Divide by $2! = 2$.
byKey.square: $8 \times 8$ pairs a team with itself and counts each pair twice.
byKey.times-two: You multiplied 8 by 2. A pair is 2 of the 8 teams, which is 8 choose 2.

explain.text: In order there are $8 \times 7 = 56$ picks of two teams. Each pair appears twice, so there are $56 \div 2 = 28$ pairs.

parts.question: Using 28 pairs, how many matches are played in a season?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Each pair of teams meets twice.

byKey.half: You halved the pairs. Each pair plays twice, so double them.
byKey.carried: That doubles 56 pairs. With 28 pairs the season has $28 \times 2 = 56$ matches.

explain.text: Each pair meets once at each ground, so $28 \times 2 = 56$ matches. A match is an ordered choice of home team then away team: $P(8, 2) = 8 \times 7 = 56$.

parts.question: The league grows. Next season has 72 matches, still home and away. Using matches $= n(n - 1)$ for $n$ teams, how many teams are there?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the whole number $n$ with $n(n - 1) = 72$.

byKey.halved: That is $72 \div 2$. Look for two whole numbers in a row whose product is 72.
byKey.one-factor: 8 is $n - 1$, the number of opponents. The number of teams is one more: $9 \times 8 = 72$.

explain.text: A season with $n$ teams has $n(n - 1)$ matches, as in part 2. Try whole numbers: $8 \times 7 = 56$ is too few and $9 \times 8 = 72$ fits. So there are 9 teams.

parts.question: With the 9 teams from part 3, the league picks 6 for a pre-season cup, all as equals. How many groups of 6 are possible?

feedback.correct: Choosing 6 to play is choosing 3 to leave out: $\binom{9}{6} = \binom{9}{3} = \dfrac{9 \times 8 \times 7}{6} = 84$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The 6 teams are equals, so order does not matter.

byKey.ordered: That is $P(9, 6)$, which ranks the 6 teams. Divide by the $6!$ orders of each group.
byKey.no-divide: $9 \times 8 \times 7 = 504$ picks the 3 left out in order. Divide by $3! = 6$.
byKey.times: You multiplied 9 by 6. A group of 6 from 9 is 9 choose 6.

explain.text: Each group of 6 in the cup leaves exactly 3 teams out, so $\binom{9}{6} = \binom{9}{3}$. That is $\dfrac{9 \times 8 \times 7}{3!} = \dfrac{504}{6} = 84$ groups.

items.prose: An ice-cream van sells 14 flavours. A cup holds 3 scoops of different flavours, and the order in the cup does not matter. A cone holds 3 scoops of different flavours stacked up, so the order from bottom to top matters.

parts.question: How many different cups are there?

feedback.generic: Not quite. In a cup the order does not matter, so count each set of flavours once.

byKey.ordered: $14 \times 13 \times 12 = 2184$ counts each cup once for every order of its scoops. Divide by $3! = 6$.
byKey.repeats: $14^3 = 2744$ lets one flavour fill two scoops. The scoops are different flavours.
byKey.times: You multiplied 14 by 3. Choosing 3 of 14 is $\binom{14}{3}$.

explain.text: In order there are $14 \times 13 \times 12 = 2184$ picks. Each set of 3 flavours turns up in $3! = 6$ orders. So there are $2184 \div 6 = 364$ cups.

parts.question: Using 364 sets of flavours, how many different cones are there?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Each set of flavours can be stacked in several orders.

byKey.times-three: You multiplied by 3. Three scoops stack in $3 \times 2 \times 1 = 6$ orders.
byKey.added: You added 6 to 364. Every set goes with every order, so multiply: $364 \times 6$.
byKey.carried: That is $2184 \times 6$, from 2184 cups in part 1. With 364 sets it is $364 \times 6 = 2184$.

explain.text: A cone is a set of flavours in an order. There are 364 sets and $3! = 6$ orders, so $364 \times 6 = 2184$ cones. Directly, $P(14, 3) = 14 \times 13 \times 12 = 2184$.

parts.question: A customer buys one item: a cup or a cone. Using 364 cups and 2184 cones, how many different items can she choose from?

feedback.generic: Not quite. She buys one item, taken from one list or the other.

byKey.multiplied: $364 \times 2184$ counts a cup and a cone together. She buys one item, so add.
byKey.carried: That adds 2184 cups and 13104 cones, from earlier slips. With 364 and 2184 it is $364 + 2184 = 2548$.

explain.text: Multiplying is for one choice after another. Here she makes one choice from two separate lists, so the counts add: $364 + 2184 = 2548$.

parts.question: Every item also comes with one of 4 toppings or with no topping. Using 2548 items, how many different purchases can she make?

feedback.correct: Five topping choices for each item: $2548 \times 5 = 12740$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The topping is a stage after the item. Count its choices with care.

byKey.no-none: That is $2548 \times 4$. No topping is a fifth choice, so multiply by 5.
byKey.added: You added 5. Every item goes with every topping choice, so multiply: $2548 \times 5$.
byKey.carried: That is $794976 \times 5$, carried from part 3. With 2548 items it is $2548 \times 5 = 12740$.

explain.text: The topping stage has $4 + 1 = 5$ choices, whatever the item. So the purchases number $2548 \times 5 = 12740$.
